ch18.title: John, the Voice in the Wilderness
ch18.b001: The Only Son in the City of Judah
ch18.b002: John the Baptist was born on March 25, 7 B.C., in fulfillment of the promise Gabriel had made to Elizabeth in June of the year before. Apart from Gabriel’s visit and an unusual dream that came to Zacharias some six weeks before the birth, there was nothing unusual or supernatural about it. On the eighth day the child was circumcised according to Jewish custom, and he grew up as an ordinary boy, day by day and year by year, in the little village then called the City of Judah, about four miles west of Jerusalem. The great event of his early childhood was a visit with his parents to Jesus and the Nazareth family in June of 1 B.C., when he was a little over six years old.
ch18.b003: There was no synagogue school in the village, but Zacharias, as a priest, was fairly well educated, and Elizabeth, herself a descendant of the “daughters of Aaron,” was far better educated than most Judean women. Since John was their only child, they gave a great deal of time to his mental and spiritual training. Zacharias served only short periods at the temple and devoted much of his time to teaching his son. The family raised sheep on a small farm, and Zacharias received a regular allowance from the temple funds.
ch18.b005: When John was fourteen, his parents took him down to Engedi by the Dead Sea, the southern headquarters of the Nazarite brotherhood, and there the boy was solemnly inducted into the order for life. He vowed to abstain from all intoxicating drink, to let his hair grow, and to refrain from touching the dead; then the family went up to Jerusalem, where John made the offerings required before the temple. These were the same life vows taken by Samson and the prophet Samuel. The Jews regarded a life Nazarite with almost the veneration they gave the high priest, for such Nazarites were the only persons besides high priests ever permitted to enter the holy of holies. At sixteen, after reading about Elijah, John was so impressed with the prophet of Mount Carmel that he adopted his style of dress, and from that day he always wore a hairy garment with a leather girdle. He was already more than six feet tall, and with his flowing hair and strange clothing he was indeed a picturesque youth.
ch18.b006: In July of A.D. 12, when John was just past eighteen, Zacharias died after an illness of several months. It was a time of great embarrassment for the young man, since his vow forbade contact with the dead, even in his own family. He had tried to keep the restriction, but he doubted that he had been wholly obedient; so after the burial he went to Jerusalem and, in the Nazarite corner of the women’s court, offered the sacrifices required for his cleansing. In September he and Elizabeth journeyed to Nazareth to visit Mary and Jesus. John had nearly made up his mind to launch out on his lifework, but by Jesus’ words and example he was persuaded to go home, take care of his mother, and await the “coming of the Father’s hour.” When he said good-bye at the end of that happy visit, he did not see Jesus again until the day of the baptism in the Jordan.
ch18.b008: Because John refused the priest’s allowance due him from the temple funds, by the end of two years he and his mother had all but lost their home. The summer he turned twenty, they moved south to Hebron with their flock. In the so-called “wilderness of Judea” John tended his sheep along a brook that fed a larger stream running down to the Dead Sea at Engedi. Along that little valley he built no fewer than a dozen stone shelters and night corrals of piled-up rock. With him lived Ezda, an orphan boy of Beth-zur whom he had in a way adopted, and who kept the herds when John went to Hebron to see his mother or down to Engedi for the Sabbath. The two lived very simply on mutton, goat’s milk, wild honey, and the edible locusts of the region. As time went on, John went less often to Hebron and more often to Engedi. He was so different from most of the Nazarites that he found it hard to fraternize with them, but he was very fond of Abner, the head of the Engedi colony.
ch18.b009: A shepherd’s life gave him much time to think. Elizabeth kept him informed of the affairs of Palestine and the world, and his conviction grew that the old order was soon to end and that he was to be the herald of a new age, “the kingdom of heaven.” He was very partial to the Prophet Daniel and read a thousand times the description of the great image which, his father had told him, stood for the kingdoms of the world from Babylon to Rome. And he read: “⟦Q 135:3.2⟧in the days of these kings shall the God of heaven set up a kingdom which shall never be destroyed.⟦/Q⟧” Yet he never fully rose above the confusion between such passages—“⟦Q 135:3.3⟧one like the Son of Man came with the clouds of heaven⟦/Q⟧”—and what his parents had told him of Jesus, or what Jesus himself had said to him at eighteen. Through it all his mother assured him that his distant cousin, Jesus of Nazareth, was the true Messiah, come to sit on the throne of David, and that John was to be his advance herald and chief support. Hearing of the vice of Rome and the evil doings of Herod Antipas, he felt that the end of the age was at hand, and he fairly vibrated with the impulse to go out and proclaim to all men: “⟦Q 135:3.4⟧Repent! Get right with God! Get ready for the end.⟦/Q⟧”
ch18.b011: On August 17, A.D. 22, when John was twenty-eight, his mother died suddenly. Knowing his vow, her friends made all the arrangements for her burial before sending for him. After the funeral he gave his flocks to the brotherhood at Engedi and for a season withdrew from the world to fast and pray. For two and a half years he lived at Engedi and persuaded most of the brotherhood that “⟦Q 135:4.3⟧the end of the age was at hand.⟦/Q⟧” He read and reread the last five chapters of Isaiah, and in Malachi he found the words: “⟦Q 135:4.4⟧Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet before the coming of the great and dreadful day of the Lord.⟦/Q⟧” This promise alone held him back for more than two years. He knew he was not Elijah. What did Malachi mean? At last he dared to think that, as the first of the prophets was called Elijah, so the last might come to bear the same name; yet his doubts were strong enough that he never called himself Elijah.
ch18.b012: Still, it was Elijah’s influence that made him attack the sins of his contemporaries so directly and bluntly. He dressed like Elijah and tried to speak like him. He was not illiterate, for he knew the sacred writings well, but he was hardly cultured. He was a clear thinker, a powerful speaker, and a fiery denunciator—hardly an example to his age, but an eloquent rebuke. And the age was ready for him. For almost a hundred years Israel had been unable to explain its subjugation to gentile overlords. The apocalyptists taught that the nation was paying for its sins, that its discipline was almost over, and that the kingdoms of this world were about to become the kingdom of God. Whether they looked for a son of David or for a new heaven and a new earth, all agreed that the kingdom was near, even at the door. At last John settled that he was to be the herald of the Messiah. He swept aside his doubts, and one day in March of A.D. 25 he left Engedi to begin his short but brilliant career as a public preacher.
ch18.b014: He went around the western shore of the Dead Sea and up the Jordan to the ancient ford opposite Jericho, where Joshua and the children of Israel had crossed into the promised land. Crossing to the far side, he took his stand near the entrance to the ford, the busiest of all the Jordan crossings, and began to preach to the travelers passing back and forth. He came from the herdsmen, like Amos. He was dressed like Elijah of old, and he thundered his warnings in the “spirit and power of Elijah.” Most who heard him went away believing they had heard the voice of a prophet, and the news spread through all Palestine. There was something new besides: he baptized every one of his believers in the Jordan “for the remission of sins.” Gentile proselytes had long been baptized, but never had Jews themselves been asked to submit to the baptism of repentance. In the fifteen months before his arrest he baptized well over one hundred thousand penitents.
ch18.b015: He preached four months at Bethany ford, and tens of thousands came from Judea, Perea, and Samaria to hear him. In May the priests and Levites sent a delegation to ask whether he claimed to be the Messiah and by whose authority he preached. John answered: “⟦Q 135:6.6⟧Go tell your masters that you have heard ‘the voice of one crying in the wilderness,’ as spoken by the prophet, saying, ‘make ready the way of the Lord, make straight a highway for our God.’⟦/Q⟧” He was a heroic but tactless preacher. When a group of Pharisees and Sadducees came forward for baptism, he said to them: “⟦Q 135:6.7⟧Who warned you to flee, as vipers before the fire, from the wrath to come? … Tell me not that Abraham is your father. I declare that God is able of these twelve stones here before you to raise up worthy children for Abraham.⟦/Q⟧” The twelve stones were the memorial stones reputedly set up by Joshua at that very crossing. Yet he also taught his disciples patiently. He told the rich to feed the poor; to the tax gatherers he said, “⟦Q 135:6.8⟧Extort no more than that which is assigned you,⟦/Q⟧” and to the soldiers, “⟦Q 135:6.8⟧Do no violence and exact nothing wrongfully—be content with your wages.⟦/Q⟧”
ch18.b016: Then he began to move north up the Jordan. The longer he preached, the more confused he became about the nature of the kingdom and its king; but he never doubted that the kingdom was coming soon. In mind John might be confused, but in spirit never. He thought much about Jesus as he went. At Adam, when his disciples asked him directly, “Are you the Messiah?” he first spoke of another to come: “⟦Q 135:7.2⟧There will come after me one who is greater than I, whose sandal straps I am not worthy to stoop down and unloose. I baptize you with water, but he will baptize you with the Holy Spirit.⟦/Q⟧”
ch18.b018: By December of A.D. 25, when John reached the neighborhood of Pella, his work was the chief topic of conversation in all the towns around the lake of Galilee. James and John, the sons of Zebedee, had gone down to be baptized, and each week they visited him and carried fresh reports back to Jesus. John asked them about Jesus and expected day by day to see him come, but he did not expect to meet him in the line of those waiting for baptism. Yet at noon on January 14, A.D. 26, there he stood, and John baptized him together with his brothers James and Jude. A voice was heard, and Jesus, his face greatly changed, came up out of the water in silence and went toward the hills to the east. John followed him far enough to tell him the story of Gabriel’s visit, as he had heard it so often from his mother, and said, “⟦Q 135:8.7⟧Now I know of a certainty that you are the Deliverer.⟦/Q⟧” But Jesus made no reply.
ch18.b019: The forty days that followed were tense for John and his disciples. Would the Messiah be a Davidic king who would smite the Romans, or had he come to establish a spiritual kingdom? John leaned, with the minority, toward the second. When some of his disciples wanted to send out parties to search for Jesus, he forbade it, saying: “⟦Q 135:9.6⟧Our times are in the hands of the God of heaven; he will direct his chosen Son.⟦/Q⟧” A new deputation from Jerusalem asked whether he was Elijah, or the prophet, or the Messiah, and to each question he answered, “I am not.” Then, early on the Sabbath morning of February 23, as the company sat at breakfast, they looked north and saw Jesus coming toward them. John stood on a large rock and lifted his sonorous voice: “⟦Q 135:9.7⟧Behold the Son of God, the deliverer of the world!⟦/Q⟧” The next morning Jesus left for Galilee. To John’s questions about his own mission he said only, “⟦Q 135:9.9⟧My Father will guide you now and in the future as he has in the past.⟦/Q⟧” The two great men parted that morning on the banks of the Jordan, never again to greet each other in the flesh.
ch18.b021: John turned south again. About a quarter of his followers had gone to Galilee in search of Jesus. A sadness of confusion hung over him; he never preached again as he had before the baptism, for he felt that the responsibility for the kingdom was no longer on his shoulders. Lonely and disconsolate, he nonetheless went on preaching and baptizing. Near Adam he made his memorable attack on Herod Antipas for unlawfully taking another man’s wife, and his preaching changed more and more into a proclamation of mercy for the common people, while he denounced the corrupt rulers with new vehemence. Herod, fearing rebellion and resenting the criticism of his domestic affairs, had him seized very early on the morning of June 12, A.D. 26, at Bethany ford, before the crowds arrived, and took him to the fortress prison of Machaerus.
ch18.b022: For more than a year and a half this rugged man of God’s outdoors languished in that despicable prison. He longed to see Jesus, and he was often tempted to doubt: if Jesus were the Messiah, why did he do nothing to set him free? When some of his disciples complained that the one he had baptized was prospering, feasting even with publicans and sinners, and doing nothing for his deliverance, John answered them: “⟦Q 135:11.2⟧He who has the bride is the bridegroom, but the friend of the bridegroom who stands near by and hears him rejoices greatly because of the bridegroom’s voice. This, my joy, therefore is fulfilled. He must increase but I must decrease.⟦/Q⟧” The disciples went away in silence, and John himself was much agitated, for he perceived that he had uttered a prophecy. Never again did he wholly doubt the mission and divinity of Jesus. Jesus loved John greatly; but knowing that John’s work on earth was finished, and knowing the great things prepared for him beyond this world, he restrained himself from interfering with the natural outworking of his career.
ch18.b023: A few days before his death, John sent messengers once more: “⟦Q 135:11.4⟧Is my work done? Why do I languish in prison? Are you truly the Messiah, or shall we look for another?⟦/Q⟧” Jesus replied that he had not forgotten, but that John must suffer this also; that the poor were having good tidings preached to them; and that “⟦Q 135:11.4⟧he shall be abundantly blessed in the age to come if he finds no occasion to doubt and stumble over me.⟦/Q⟧” This was the last word John received from Jesus, and it greatly comforted him.
ch18.b024: Herod feared to release John lest he stir up rebellion, and feared to kill him lest the thousands of Pereans who held him a prophet should riot. Several times he talked with John about the kingdom of heaven and was sometimes seriously impressed, yet he dared not let him go. Herodias, Herod’s unlawful wife, hated John bitterly. At a great birthday feast in the palace at Machaerus, she sent her daughter to dance before the banqueters. Herod, well under the influence of his wines, promised the girl whatever she desired, “⟦Q 135:12.6⟧even to the half of my kingdom.⟦/Q⟧” She went aside to ask her mother, then came back and said, “⟦Q 135:12.6⟧I request that you forthwith give me the head of John the Baptist on a platter.⟦/Q⟧” Herod was filled with fear and sorrow, but because of his oath and his guests he would not refuse. That night John was beheaded in the prison. When his disciples heard of it, they came for his body, laid it in a tomb, and went and told Jesus.
ch19.title: The Baptism in the Jordan
ch19.b002: Jesus began his public work at the very height of popular interest in John’s preaching, at a time when the Jews of Palestine were eagerly watching for the Messiah. Yet the two men could hardly have been more different. John was an eager and earnest worker; Jesus was a calm and happy laborer, and only a few times in his whole life was he ever in a hurry. Jesus was a comforting consolation to the world; John was hardly a comfort. He preached the kingdom of heaven but hardly entered into its happiness. When John proclaimed the coming kingdom, the burden of his message was: Repent! Flee from the wrath to come. When Jesus began to preach, the call to repentance remained, but it was always followed by the gospel, the good tidings of the joy and liberty of the new kingdom.
ch19.b004: The Jews held many ideas about the expected deliverer, and each school could point to passages in the Hebrew scriptures to support its view. In earlier times they had pictured him as “the servant of the Lord,” then as “the Son of Man,” and lately some had even called him the “Son of God.” The more learned imagined him as the perfected and representative Israelite, uniting in himself the threefold office of prophet, priest, and king. They devoutly believed that as Moses had delivered their fathers from Egypt by miraculous wonders, so the Messiah would deliver them from Rome by even greater miracles of power. The rabbis had gathered almost five hundred passages they held to be Messianic prophecies, and amid all their details of time and technique they almost completely lost sight of the personality of the promised one. They looked for the restoration of Israel’s national glory rather than for the salvation of the world, and so Jesus of Nazareth could never satisfy their materialistic hope.
ch19.b005: Most Jews believed that they still languished under Roman rule because of their national sins. The nation had not wholeheartedly repented, and therefore the Messiah delayed his coming. That was why John’s preaching—“⟦Q 136:1.5⟧Repent and be baptized, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand⟦/Q⟧”—had so mighty and immediate an appeal. To any devout Jew the kingdom of heaven could mean only one thing: the coming of the Messiah.
ch19.b006: But there was one feature of Michael’s bestowal that was utterly foreign to every Jewish idea of the Messiah: the union of the two natures, the human and the divine. The Jews had imagined the Messiah as perfected human, as superhuman, even as divine, but never as human and divine joined in one earth personality. This would be the great stumbling block of Jesus’ early disciples. The incarnation of the Creator in the form of the creature had not been revealed beforehand. It was revealed only in Jesus; the world knew nothing of such things until the Creator Son was made flesh and dwelt among the mortals of the realm.
ch19.b008: As the news of John filled the towns around the lake, Jesus’ brothers James and Jude began to talk of going down to be baptized. On Saturday night, January 12, A.D. 26, after hearing Jesus speak in the synagogue at Capernaum, the two asked his counsel about their plans. He asked them to wait until the next day for his answer. That night he slept very little, being in close communion with the Father in heaven.
ch19.b009: On Sunday morning Jesus was at work in the boatshop as usual. He had arranged to have lunch with his brothers at noon, and James and Jude arrived with the food and waited in the lumber room, knowing how regular he was about the midday rest. Just before the noon hour, Jesus laid down his tools, took off his work apron, and simply announced to the three workmen in the room with him, “My hour has come.” He went out to his brothers and said again, “⟦Q 135:8.3⟧My hour has come—let us go to John.⟦/Q⟧” They set out at once for Pella, eating their lunch as they walked. That night they rested in the Jordan valley, and they arrived at the place of John’s baptizing about noon the next day.
ch19.b011: John had just begun the day’s baptisms. Scores of penitents stood in line along the bank, and Jesus and his two brothers took their places among these earnest men and women. John had been asking Zebedee’s sons about Jesus and had expected day by day to see him arrive, but he had not expected to meet him among the candidates. So busy was he with the rapid baptizing of so many converts that he did not look up until the Son of Man stood directly before him. When he recognized Jesus, the ceremony halted for a moment. “⟦Q 135:8.5⟧But why do you come down into the water to greet me?⟦/Q⟧” he asked. Jesus answered, “⟦Q 135:8.5⟧To be subject to your baptism.⟦/Q⟧” John replied: “⟦Q 135:8.5⟧But I have need to be baptized by you. Why do you come to me?⟦/Q⟧” And Jesus whispered to him: “⟦Q 135:8.5⟧Bear with me now, for it becomes us to set this example for my brothers standing here with me, and that the people may know that my hour has come.⟦/Q⟧”
ch19.b012: There was a tone of finality and authority in Jesus’ voice. Trembling with emotion, John baptized Jesus of Nazareth in the Jordan at noon on Monday, January 14, A.D. 26, and then his brothers James and Jude. This was in no sense a rite of repentance or a baptism for the remission of sins. The Jews believed that the sin of one person might curse the whole nation, and many devout souls came to John for the good of Israel, fearing that some sin of ignorance on their part might delay the Messiah’s coming. In accepting baptism Jesus was only following the example of these pious Israelites. He repented of no misdeeds and confessed no sin. His was the baptism of consecration to the doing of the heavenly Father’s will. When John had baptized the three, he dismissed the others for the day and announced that he would begin again at noon the next day.
ch19.b014: When Jesus went down into the Jordan, he was a mortal of the realm who had reached the pinnacle of human ascension in the conquest of mind and in self-identification with the spirit. Perfect synchrony and full communication had been established between his mortal mind and the indwelling Adjuster, the divine gift of his Father in Paradise. Ordinarily, when a mortal attains such heights, the matured soul fuses with its divine Adjuster, and many superhuman observers expected to witness just that on this day. They were disappointed, for something new and even greater occurred. As John laid his hands upon Jesus to baptize him, the indwelling Adjuster took final leave of the perfected human soul of Joshua ben Joseph. And in a few moments this divine entity returned from Divinington as a Personalized Adjuster, chief of his kind throughout the whole local universe of Nebadon.
ch19.b015: As the people were leaving, the four men still standing in the water heard a strange sound, and for a moment an apparition appeared just above the head of Jesus. They heard a voice saying, “⟦Q 136:2.3⟧This is my beloved Son in whom I am well pleased.⟦/Q⟧” John and the two brothers heard these words, but John’s disciples on the bank neither heard them nor saw anything. Only the eyes of Jesus beheld the Personalized Adjuster. It was the Adjuster’s voice they heard, speaking on behalf of the Universal Father, for the Adjuster is of, and as, the Paradise Father; and for the rest of his earth life this exalted Adjuster was with Jesus in all his labors, in constant communion with him. When the voice had spoken, all was silence. While the four of them lingered in the water, Jesus looked up to the near-by Adjuster and prayed:
ch19.b017: When he had prayed, the “heavens were opened,” and the Son of Man saw a vision of himself as a Son of God, as he had been before he came to earth in the likeness of mortal flesh, and as he would be when the incarnated life was finished. This heavenly vision was seen by Jesus alone. At his baptism he heard the unmistakable call of his Father, the final summons to be about his Father’s business. That day ended the purely human life of Jesus. The divine Son had found his Father, the Universal Father had found his incarnated Son, and they spoke the one to the other.
ch19.b018: Jesus was then almost thirty-one and a half years old. Luke says that he was baptized in the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar, but Tiberius had been coemperor with Augustus for two and a half years before Augustus died, so that the fifteenth year of his actual rule was this very year, A.D. 26. It was also the year that Pontius Pilate began his rule as governor of Judea.
ch19.b019: A great change came over the face of Jesus. Coming up out of the water in silence, he took leave of them and walked away toward the hills to the east. And no man saw Jesus again for forty days.
ch20.title: Forty Days and Six Decisions
ch20.b002: After his baptism Jesus withdrew from men for forty days. He had already endured the great temptation of his mortal bestowal before the baptism, when for six weeks he had been wet with the dews of Mount Hermon; there, as an unaided mortal, he had met and defeated Caligastia, the pretender prince of this world. This new retirement was not a struggle with temptation. It was a time to adjust himself to the changed relationships of the world and the universe brought about by the personalization of his Adjuster, and to formulate the plans and methods for proclaiming the new kingdom of God in the hearts of men. Nor did he go into the hills to fast and afflict his soul. He was not an ascetic, and he came forever to destroy all such notions about the approach to God.
ch20.b003: Jesus was now wholly self-conscious of his relation to the universe of his making and to the universe of universes supervised by the Paradise Father. He fully recalled the bestowal charge and the instructions given him by his elder brother, Immanuel, before he entered upon his Urantia incarnation, and he wanted a season of quiet meditation to think out the plans for his public labors on behalf of this world and of all the other worlds of his local universe. Wandering through the Perean hills in search of shelter, he settled in an ancient rock cavern in the hillside near a village sometime called Beit Adis, and he drank from a small spring that came out of the hill close by. Throughout these forty days James and John, the sons of Zebedee, searched for him. Many times they passed not far from his shelter, but they never found him.
ch20.b005: While wandering in the hills, Jesus met his universe chief executive, Gabriel, the Bright and Morning Star of Nebadon. It was the first time they had met directly since Michael took leave of his associates on Salvington to begin the Urantia bestowal. By direction of Immanuel and on the authority of the Ancients of Days, Gabriel informed Jesus that his bestowal was practically finished so far as earning the perfected sovereignty of his universe and ending the Lucifer rebellion were concerned. The first had been achieved on the day of his baptism, when the personalization of his Adjuster demonstrated the completion of his bestowal in the likeness of mortal flesh. The second had become a fact of history on the day he came down from Mount Hermon to join the waiting lad, Tiglath.
ch20.b006: While they talked on the mountain, the Constellation Father of Edentia appeared to them in person and said: “⟦Q 136:3.5⟧The records are completed. The sovereignty of Michael number 611,121 over his universe of Nebadon rests in completion at the right hand of the Universal Father.⟦/Q⟧” He brought Immanuel’s release of the bestowal: Jesus was free, now or at any later time and in any manner he chose, to end his incarnation, ascend to the right hand of his Father, and assume his well-earned rulership of all Nebadon. “⟦Q 136:3.5⟧Technically, your work on Urantia and in the flesh of the mortal creature is finished. Your course from now on is a matter of your own choosing.⟦/Q⟧” When the Most High Father had gone, Jesus talked long with Gabriel about the welfare of the universe, and he sent greetings to Immanuel with the assurance that in the work he was about to undertake he would always remember the counsel he had received on Salvington.
ch20.b008: Day by day, up in the hills, Jesus laid his plans for the rest of his bestowal. He decided first not to teach at the same time as John. He would stay in comparative retirement until John’s work had achieved its purpose or until John was suddenly stopped by imprisonment, for he knew well that John’s fearless and tactless preaching would soon arouse the fears and enmity of the civil rulers. Then he reviewed Immanuel’s instructions, among them the advice that he should leave no permanent writing on the planet. Never again did Jesus write on anything except sand. On his next visit to Nazareth, much to the sorrow of his brother Joseph, he destroyed all his writing that was preserved on the boards about the carpenter shop and on the walls of the old home.
ch20.b009: He did not fast during these forty days. For the first two days he was so absorbed in thought that he forgot to eat, but on the third day he went in search of food. Nor was he tempted during this time by any evil spirits or rebel personalities. These forty days were the first real functioning of the human and the divine minds as now made one, and their outcome showed that the divine mind had triumphantly and spiritually dominated the human intellect. From this time on, though the selfhood of the human mind was always present, that spiritualized mind always said, “⟦Q 136:4.4⟧Not my will but yours be done.⟦/Q⟧” Gabriel had made clear that he might order the rest of his life in either of two ways: his own way, or the Father’s way. On the third day of his isolation Jesus promised himself that he would go back to the world to finish his career, and that whenever two ways lay before him he would always choose the Father’s will. These were not days of great temptation, but of the Master’s great decisions.
ch20.b010: The First Decision · The Heavenly Hosts
ch20.b011: On the third day Jesus was shown the vision of the assembled celestial hosts of Nebadon, sent by their commanders to wait upon the will of their beloved Sovereign: twelve legions of seraphim and proportionate numbers of every order of universe intelligence. The first great decision of his isolation concerned whether he would use these mighty beings in his public work on Urantia. He decided that he would not use a single one of them unless it should become evident that this was his Father’s will. The host remained with him to the end, always ready to obey the least expression of their Sovereign’s will, and Jesus placed their immediate command in the hands of his Personalized Adjuster.
ch20.b012: In accepting this command, the Adjuster took great pains to point out one thing. He could limit these beings perfectly in all matters of space, but not in matters of time, for once personalized, Adjusters are nontime beings. “⟦Q 136:5.4⟧If your united natures once entertain such desires, these mandates of your choice will be forthwith executed. … In my self-consciousness time is nonexistent, and therefore I cannot limit your creatures in anything related thereto.⟦/Q⟧” So, unless the Father in heaven ruled otherwise, any supernatural accompaniment of Jesus’ ministry would pertain wholly to the elimination of time. To prevent the appearance of time miracles, Jesus had to remain constantly time conscious.
ch20.b013: The Second Decision · Stones and Bread
ch20.b014: Then Jesus turned his thoughts toward himself. What would he, the fully self-conscious creator of all things in this universe, do with his creator prerogatives in the daily situations he would face? The problem had already presented itself in those lonely hills, for by the third day his body was hungry. Should he go in search of food as any ordinary man would, or simply exercise his creative powers and produce nourishment ready at hand? This decision has been portrayed as a temptation, a challenge to “⟦Q 136:6.1⟧command that these stones become loaves of bread.⟦/Q⟧” Jesus chose, as far as his personal needs were concerned, to follow the path of normal earthly existence. He decided not to seek self-preservation, and he put his conclusion in the words of Scripture familiar to his human mind: “⟦Q 136:6.4⟧Man shall not live by bread alone but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God.⟦/Q⟧” His superhuman power he might use for others, but for himself never; and he held to this to the very end, when it was jeeringly said of him: “⟦Q 136:6.5⟧He saved others; himself he cannot save⟦/Q⟧”—because he would not.
ch20.b015: Jesus sorrowed for his people. He understood how they had been taught to expect a Messiah who would bring miraculous plenty, a time when “⟦Q 136:6.7⟧the earth will yield its fruits ten thousandfold,⟦/Q⟧” and every grape “⟦Q 136:6.7⟧will produce a gallon of wine.⟦/Q⟧” But he was not a Messiah coming to multiply bread and wine. He came to reveal his Father in heaven to his children on earth. In this decision he showed an onlooking universe the folly and sin of prostituting divine talents for personal aggrandizement or selfish gain. That was the sin of Lucifer and Caligastia.
ch20.b016: The Third Decision · On the Ledge
ch20.b017: Next he considered what his attitude would be in the face of personal danger. He decided to exercise normal care for his human safety and take reasonable precautions against an untimely end, but to refrain from all superhuman intervention when the crisis of his life in the flesh should come. As he reached this decision, he was sitting in the shade of a tree on an overhanging ledge of rock, with a precipice right before him. He knew that he could cast himself off into space and come to no harm, if only he would undo his first two decisions. He knew the Scripture well: “⟦Q 136:7.2⟧They shall bear you up in their hands lest you dash your foot against a stone.⟦/Q⟧” But such defiance of his Father’s laws of gravity, however gratifying to the sign-seeking Jews, would be, not a revelation of his Father, but a questionable trifling with the established laws of the universe of universes. He never walked on the water. Whether the Pharisees taunted him for a sign or the watchers at Calvary dared him to come down from the cross, he held steadfastly to the decision of that hour on the hillside.
ch20.b018: The Fourth Decision · A Generation Seeking Signs
ch20.b019: Should he use any of his superhuman powers to attract the attention and win the allegiance of his fellow men? He decided that he should not. He foresaw that miracles and wonders would call forth only outward allegiance by overawing the material mind; they would neither reveal God nor save men. Even when he later permitted time-shortening ministrations of mercy, he almost always told those he healed to tell no man. There was in this dialogue a human element of questioning and near-doubting, for Jesus was man as well as God. It was plain that the Jews would never receive him as Messiah if he worked no wonders. But he decided that it would not be in keeping with the Father’s will for the divine mind to make that concession to the doubts of the human mind.
ch20.b020: He remembered Rome, Alexandria, and Damascus, and he knew how the world gained its ends by compromise and diplomacy; he would use none of it. He knew the short cuts open to one of his powers. Soon the Passover would fill Jerusalem with visitors. He could climb to the pinnacle of the temple and, before the bewildered multitude, walk out on the air; that was just the kind of Messiah they were looking for. But he had not come to re-establish David’s throne. Jesus chose to establish the kingdom of heaven in men’s hearts by natural, ordinary, difficult, and trying methods, the very methods his earth children must later follow, for well did the Son of Man know that it would be “⟦Q 136:8.6⟧through much tribulation that many of the children of all ages would enter into the kingdom.⟦/Q⟧”
ch20.b022: Last he considered how he should proclaim and establish the kingdom. The Jews looked for a deliverer who would come in miraculous power, cast down Israel’s enemies, and make the Jews rulers of the world. Jesus knew the kingdom of heaven had to do with the overthrow of evil in the hearts of men. You can hardly imagine what would have happened on Urantia had this God-man, now in potential possession of all power in heaven and on earth, decided to unfurl the banner of sovereignty and marshal wonder-working battalions. But he would not compromise with the revolutionary techniques of Caligastia. He would proclaim to an onlooking universe, “⟦Q 136:9.3⟧You shall worship the Lord your God and him only shall you serve.⟦/Q⟧” The idea of battle and slaughter was repugnant to him; before his baptism he had again refused the Zealots’ offer to lead them against Rome. Now he concluded that the Scriptures his mother had taught him—“⟦Q 136:9.7⟧You shall break them with a rod of iron⟦/Q⟧”—did not refer to him. Once and for all his human mind swept away the tangle of Hebrew scriptures, parental training, chazan teaching, Jewish expectations, and human ambition. He would return to Galilee, quietly begin to proclaim the kingdom, and trust his Father to work out the details day by day.
ch20.b023: He would not deal out bread to the multitudes, as he had so recently seen done in Rome. He would not draw attention to himself by wonder-working, nor seek to win acceptance for a spiritual message by political authority or temporal power. By rejecting these methods he made certain that the Jews would finally reject his claims, and knowing this, he long tried to keep his early followers from calling him the Messiah. Throughout his public ministry he would face three recurring demands: the clamor to be fed, the insistence on miracles, and the final request that he allow his followers to make him king. But he never departed from the decisions made in the Perean hills.
ch20.b024: On the last day of his isolation, before starting down the mountain to join John and his disciples, the Son of Man made his final decision, and he spoke it to the Personalized Adjuster:
ch20.b026: Then he went down the mountain, and his face shone with the glory of spiritual victory and moral achievement.
